lessons.title: Why AI is used and what it needs
lessons.html:
Artificial insemination on the farm

Artificial insemination (AI) means placing semen from a selected sire into the female's reproductive tract by hand, without a bull, ram or boar being present. It is widely used in South African dairy herds, in stud beef herds and in pig units, and increasingly in sheep and goats.

Benefits

  • Access to proven top sires from South Africa and overseas at the cost of a straw of semen.
  • Faster genetic improvement in milk, growth or carcass traits.
  • Fewer bulls to feed and handle, which is safer and cheaper.
  • Less spread of venereal diseases such as trichomoniasis and vibriosis.
  • Planned calving seasons and better records.

Requirements for success

AI only works when several things are right at the same time: the female is cycling and in good body condition, heat is detected accurately, semen has been stored and thawed correctly, and a trained inseminator places it at the right time and place. If one link fails, conception rates fall.

Only trained and authorised people should inseminate. Your role as supervisor is to plan the program, make sure heat detection is done well, control the semen tank and records, check hygiene and animal handling, and follow up on results. Work closely with the farm's vet and the AI company.

Synchronisation

Many farms use hormone programs to bring a group of females into heat together, so that they can be inseminated on fixed days. These products are prescribed by a vet and must be used exactly as the vet instructs. Record every injection and device with the date and animal number.

lessons.title: Heat detection, semen handling and insemination
lessons.html:
Detecting heat

Missed or wrong heats are the biggest cause of poor AI results. Cows should be watched carefully at least twice a day, early morning and late afternoon, for about 20–30 minutes each time.

  • Standing heat – the cow stands still when mounted by another cow. This is the main sign.
  • Other signs – restlessness, mounting others, clear mucus from the vulva, swollen vulva, bellowing, drop in milk.
  • Aids – tail paint or chalk, heat mount detectors, pedometers or activity collars.

A common guide is the AM–PM rule: a cow first seen in standing heat in the morning is inseminated that afternoon, and one first seen in the afternoon is inseminated the next morning. Follow the farm's protocol.

Semen tank and thawing

  1. Keep the liquid nitrogen tank in a cool, ventilated place and check the nitrogen level weekly. Record it.
  2. Lift the canister only to the neck of the tank, and only for a few seconds, using tweezers to remove a straw.
  3. Thaw the straw in a water bath at the temperature the AI company specifies, for the time it specifies, and protect it from cold and sunlight.
  4. Inseminate soon after thawing.

Safety with liquid nitrogen

Liquid nitrogen is extremely cold and causes severe cold burns. Wear gloves and eye protection when filling the tank or lifting canisters. Never close it in an airtight container and never use it in a small closed room, because the gas can push out oxygen.

Hygiene and handling

Restrain the cow in a crush or AI box calmly. Clean the vulva, use a new sheath and glove for each cow and keep the gun clean and dry.

lessons.title: Records and evaluating the AI program
lessons.html:
Keeping AI records

Every insemination must be recorded. Without records you cannot know the sire of a calf, the expected calving date or whether the program is working.

RecordWhy it matters
Date and time of heat and inseminationChecks timing; predicts calving date
Cow number and bull or straw codePedigree and herd book registration
Inseminator nameCompares results between people
Pregnancy test resultShows conception rate
Tank nitrogen levels and stock of strawsProtects valuable semen

Measuring results

Work out the conception rate: the number of females pregnant from first service divided by the number inseminated. Compare it by inseminator, by bull, by month and by group of animals. A sudden drop may point to a problem with semen handling, heat detection, nutrition or disease.

Common problems and actions

  • Many repeat heats at about 21 days: check timing and heat detection.
  • Irregular returns: possible early embryo loss or disease; call the vet.
  • Thin cows not cycling: improve feeding and body condition.
  • One inseminator with poor results: retrain and observe.

Plan a pregnancy test by the vet some weeks after insemination, and decide what to do with open females, for example a second AI round or a clean-up bull.

Key points

  • AI success depends on good heat detection, correct semen handling and a trained inseminator.
  • Watch for standing heat at least twice a day.
  • Handle liquid nitrogen with gloves and eye protection, in a ventilated place.
  • Record every heat, insemination, sire and pregnancy result.
  • Use conception rates to find and fix problems.
